blind_spots: Evidence skews heavily toward writers and visual artists; relatively thin first-person testimony from designers, filmmakers, and game artists despite being named in scope.

Most 'soulless' and emotional-authenticity claims come from a single Perplexity Sonar synthesis rather than independently verifiable primary quotes, so the strength of underlying primary evidence is hard to gauge.
Little evidence on pricing, learning-curve, or onboarding friction as abandonment drivers — almost all complaints are about output quality/meaning, not cost or usability.
No quantitative data on what fraction of skeptics actually returned after improvements, or which specific changes (memory, personalization) measurably re-engaged them.
Pro/positive counter-experiences (e.g., AI as useful for competitor analysis or brainstorming) are mentioned but under-explored relative to the negative cluster.
contradictions: Some creatives reject AI output as soulless and meaningless, while others report concrete value when AI is confined to mechanical tasks (e.g., the niks_df tweet on Atria's Raya earning its keep for competitor creatives + auto-tagging hooks), suggesting the problem is role/scope, not the technology itself.

Detectability of 'AI tells' is treated both as a damning flaw (generic ChatGPT-isms) and dismissed by others who embrace those markers — e.g., a user saying they love the em-dash and don't care if it reads as AI.

One thread argues for openly disclosing/normalizing AI use ('Why we should stop disclosing AI use' / 'AI Doesn't Kill Creativity'), directly opposing the dominant panel narrative that AI undermines authenticity and craft.

The 'almost useless after recent updates' complaint conflicts with a commenter's suggestion that models have improved significantly since 2021, implying disagreement over whether output quality is trending down or up.
